Painter Reggie Burrows Hodges brings a contemporary perspective to 17th-century European art in Reggie Burrows Hodges: A Theater of Passions , opening at the J. Paul Getty Museum in Los Angeles. The exhibition features paintings inspired by works in the Getty’s collection , exploring the violence and theatricality behind historical narratives. It is part of a three-venue presentation that also includes exhibitions at the California African American Museum and Art + Practice .
Born in Compton in 1965, Hodges draws on Old Master paintings to examine power, memory, and human experience. He often begins with the compositions of historical works, then reshapes their themes through his own visual language. His paintings emerge from black grounds, with figures defined by soft, gestural marks and richly rendered surroundings. The dark palettes and hazy contours evoke the uncertainty of memory, giving ordinary gestures a heightened emotional presence.
At the Getty, Hodges responds to three Italian paintings: Orazio Gentileschi’s Lot and His Daughters and Danaë and the Shower of Gold , and Artemisia Gentileschi’s Lucretia . Each work contains dramatic narratives shaped by violence, vulnerability, and power. Hodges draws out these underlying tensions through atmospheric compositions that favor psychological presence over naturalistic detail. His interpretations offer a contemporary reading of the original paintings without losing sight of their emotional complexity.
The presentation extends to the California African American Museum, where Reggie Burrows Hodges: A Theater of Miracles explores further connections to historical painting. Several works take inspiration from the Getty’s collection, including Jacopo Bassano’s 16th-century painting T he Miracle of the Quail . Hodges reworks the drama of these earlier compositions while directing attention toward the everyday gestures that give his scenes their emotional weight.

Curated by Ana Carolina Ralston, the exhibition examines how urban development reshapes collective memory and individual identity. VHILS uses acid, oxidation, and subtraction to transform corroded metal into layered compositions. The works bring together visual traces of Lisbon, São Paulo, and Shanghai. A large-scale intervention on the gallery’s glass facade also extends the exhibition into the surrounding city.
Since beginning his career in graffiti in the early 2000s, VHILS has expanded his practice to include bas-relief carving, metal etching, wood carving, sculpture, and site-specific installations. His work considers what is lost as cities change, particularly as globalization and development threaten established communities. After more than a decade of working with Brazilian communities, he returns to São Paulo with these questions at the center of his latest exhibition.
Atrito: Arqueologia do Presente opens on November 14 and runs through February 20, 2027 at Galleria Continua São Paulo.
My Modern Met had the opportunity to speak with VHILS before the opening of his exhibition. Scroll down to read our exclusive interview where he discusses the connections between cities, material and memory, and what urban environments reveal about contemporary society.

UNESCO’s largest and most well-known activity is the designation of landmarks that hold cultural or natural importance. These UNESCO World Heritage Sites are masterpieces of human creative genius and landmarks of nature. Designated as ‘patrimony’, with outstanding value to the story of humanity, there have been 1,223 sites protected across 168 countries, so far. Italy is the country with the UNESCO World Heritage Sites (60) with China closely following with 59—and Germany some distance behind at 54. The United States has 26, many of which are natural.
UNESCO has also launched global movements, such as Education For All, to further advance its core objectives of ensuring no child goes uneducated. UNESCO also plays a large role in the protection of monuments and patrimony from destruction, but natural and human-caused. At the time of writing, UNESCO’s ‘Reviving the Spirit of Mosul’ Campaign just completed a landmark restoration in the northern Iraqi city that was once the capital of ISIS.
The famous al-Nuri ‘Leaning Minaret’ of the 12th-century mosque of the same name was just rebuilt with its signature lean intact. Reviving the Spirit of Mosul has also seen over 120 heritage buildings restored from war damage according to the original plan and design of the age in which they were built, and many of them are now not only inhabited by local families, but some by the very craftsmen whose traditional skills informed their reconstruction. Tirana, Albania, has become one of Europe’s fastest-growing cities. This growth has sparked a real estate boom, but locals worry about losing green areas and public spaces. Bjarke Ingels Group (BIG) has addressed these issues with its proposal for an upcoming development on Rinia Park, in the heart of Tirana.
Named Fountain Plaza Tirana, the project won over designs presented by four other international firms. Conceived as a mixed-use building, Fountain Plaza Tirana will stand several feet above Rinia Park, preserving and expanding the public park area while making room for a new hotel, apartments, offices, and cultural spaces.
The building evokes a dense cloud formation above the park. To achieve this, layers of rounded, perforated white terraces rest on slim columns, while two wider structures at opposite ends of the building house the elevators that provide floor access. To avoid breaking with the “floating” concept, these elements are clad in flute glass to let light shine through and onto the park.
“We have reimagined urban living in three dimensions—not as a vertical extrusion or a tower competing for attention on the skyline, but as a cloud of homes hovering above the park,” said BIG founder Bjarke Ingels told Dezeen . “Rather than diminishing the park or displacing public life, the building enhances and accommodates both.”
As such, Fountain Plaza Tirana will also feature an open-access library, a covered public auditorium, and community facilities. In addition to the design that lets pedestrians move freely across the park, this aims to make the building’s ground floor a bustling gathering place for city dwellers and visitors alike.
The design also accounts for Tirana’s weather, particularly its hot summers. The structures bring shade to a public park without completely blocking sunlight. Meanwhile, the water features, described as an “inverted fountain,” can cool the area with the effect of a light drizzle. The water used comes from a closed-loop system. With this, the water collected from the building and the green areas at the bottom is stored, filtered, and returned to the park below.
While a building timeline has yet to be announced, it will surely be interesting to see how Fountain Plaza Tirana takes shape. An 81-year-old Englishman grew up wondering who his real father was. What he didn’t know was that an entire family tree in Canada was wondering who and where he was.
After being divided by a world war, an ocean, and 8 decades, Rodney Anderson has finally found his long lost relatives with the help of a simple DNA test, and a persistent, curious niece.
“I thought ‘This is a wind up.’ It has to be,” Anderson said, sharing with CBC News the moment he learned of his true origins.
“But it wasn’t. You can’t believe what a shock it is to get that knowledge.”
Anderson’s mother had a child with a visiting Canadian soldier during the Second World War, a secret that his mother and grandmother never shared with him.
He grew up with no knowledge or explanation of his father’s origins whatsoever because of the stigma attached at the time to these out-of-wedlock births, even though they came about during a period of immense crisis and uncertainty about the future.
Canadian Bethany Allen began searching in 2008 for this mystery uncle of hers after discovering in divorce papers that her grandfather, Charles Blakney, had had a child with a woman in the UK in 1944.
He had first sailed off to war in 1942, leaving behind a wife and daughter in New Brunswick. Blakney served as a motor and driver mechanic with the New Brunswick Rangers and returned home in 1945, the same year that Rodney Anderson was born in Farnham to his mother Yvonne. Rumors of his affair overseas remained in the family long after the guns fell silent in Europe.
“My mother [Rodney’s half-sister] had always wanted to know that [Anderson] had a good life and was happy,” Bethany Allen told CBC News.
It took a long time to confirm the link between the Blakney family in Canada and Anderson in Surrey. It came about through a commercial DNA test from Ancestry.

Heavy rain and rising floodwaters in Florida made parts of Save the Chimps sanctuary inaccessible. As a result, staff had to get creative to keep one of their residents supplied. Their solution was a drone, which delivered food and blankets to Kaleb, a 38-year-old chimpanzee whose outdoor area had become cut off by the water.
Between November 1 and November 3, 2026, nearly 19 inches of rain fell across the area surrounding the 150-acre sanctuary near Fort Pierce, Florida. The downpour overwhelmed nearby canals, sending water across internal roads and making it difficult for employees to reach the chimpanzees. Staff typically use golf carts to transport approximately 3,000 pounds of food around the property each day, but submerged roads made those routes impassable. A high-clearance swamp buggy initially helped employees navigate the water, but it soon broke down, forcing the team to find alternative ways to get supplies where they were needed.
Fortunately, the sanctuary had purchased a delivery drone some time earlier for emergencies just like this. Staff put it to use when they realized Kaleb became isolated in an outdoor area surrounded by floodwater. The drone carried food and blankets to him until he eventually moved on his own to a more accessible part of the property.
Footage shared by the sanctuary showed Kaleb retrieving a paper bag dropped by the drone and pulling out a banana. Luckily, he and the sanctuary’s more than 200 chimpanzees remained safe thanks to the dedication of the staff who stayed overnight to ensure the animals continued receiving care. According to the sanctuary’s facilities director, the chimpanzees continued receiving their food on schedule.
By November 7, water levels had dropped considerably, although only about 20% of the property’s roads were passable. The sanctuary has since begun assessing the damage, which includes roads requiring extensive resurfacing, damaged vehicles and equipment, and buildings in need of roof repairs and mold remediation.
Save the Chimps is now appealing to donors for help covering the recovery costs, with one supporter agreeing to match contributions. While the flooding temporarily complicated nearly every aspect of the sanctuary’s daily operations, its emergency preparations helped ensure that the chimpanzees remained safe and cared for throughout the storm.

During a Major League Baseball game between the Kansas City Royals and the Toronto Blue Jays, the best team performance didn’t take place on the field. Instead, it happened in the stands, where fans from all walks of life came together for a mouthwatering mission. All they had to do was to assemble an oversized, inflatable hot dog in a race against time.
The contest, known as “Home Bun Race,” was set up by QuickTrip, a chain of convenience stores in Midwestern, Southern, and Western United States. The objective is for fans in attendance to piece together a 10-foot-tall inflatable hot dog and equally sized bun, which were each launched from opposite sides of the stadium. If the crowd managed to unite the massive meal in under 35 seconds, there would be free hot dogs for everyone.
Though it sounds pretty straight forward, it can be tricky to coordinate and move the inflatable pieces in such a short amount of time—especially when it’s a crowd of strangers who haven’t prepared or ever worked together before. Still, the fans managed to achieve their goal, resulting in a World Series-level roar from the crowd. Although the home team lost 4-3, the fans walked away with a coupon that they could later redeem for their free treat. So… everyone won.
According to Ads of the World , QuickTrip created this campaign in partnership with Laughlin Constable, their creative and media agency. It is also the first activation of its kind in MLB, and the most successful social activation QuickTrip has ever done due to its social media reach and press coverage. In addition to Kauffman Stadium in Kansas City, the campaign has also taken place at the Cardinals stadium in St. Louis.

What began as an exciting hiking trip quickly turned into something else entirely when climbers in Greece found an orphaned seal pup on a beach at the bottom of a cliff.
Considered a Critically Endangered species in Greece, the climbers resolved to go right back up the way they came—the seal pup safely secured in a backpack.
It was stranded without its mother on the inaccessible Kalamia Beach—whose beauty and solitude were supposed to be the climbers’ reward for negotiating the rugged cliffs on the island of Kythira.
Vrettos Sklavos, from Outdoor Activities Greece said there is a sea cave near Kalamia Beach that these Mediterranean monk seals use to escape rough seas. Perhaps a big wave had separated the little fellow from its mother.
An animal rescue operation on the island wrote on Facebook that the climbers took “all the right steps,” calling (MOm) the Hellenic Society for the Study and Protection of the Mediterranean Monk Seal, the coast guard, and Animal Aid Kythira , whose veterinarians eventually descended the cliffs together with the climbers to rescue the seal.
“A huge thank you to Vrettos and his team for their immediate response,” the operation wrote on Facebook.
In an update from Keep Talking Greece , the seal is said to have arrived severely dehydrated and malnourished, weighing just 15 kilograms at 1 year old. It was determined that after a brief stay with Animal Aid Kythira it would be transported to Thessaly on the mainland before eventually arriving at the Society’s rehabilitation location in Spata.
Here, it will receive round-the-clock care with the aim of attempting to preserve enough of its wild intuition and nature as to permit a return to the sea when the time is right.

Being a paramedic takes a special kind of person. It calls for compassion, resilience, and the ability to stay calm when others are at their most vulnerable. Just one day on the job can take its toll, yet Durham, California-based paramedic Mike Nevill dedicated an incredible 59 years to the vital role. A recent viral video captures a heartwarming tribute made to Nevill as he sits in his ambulance for the last time before retiring.
As Nevill sits in the driver’s seat, he listens to a radio tribute from the dispatch team thanking him for his dedication and reflecting on his extraordinary career. Outside the ambulance, community members gather to show their support, while Nevill appears visibly emotional. The tribute also highlights how Nevill inspired his own daughter to follow in his footsteps and become a paramedic, “carrying forward the Nevill family tradition of caring for others.”
When sharing the video on Instagram , Durham Region Paramedic Services wrote in the caption, “Beginning his career in 1967, Mike dedicated a lifetime to caring for others, serving as a paramedic, supervisor, mentor and leader. His commitment extended beyond Durham, with decades of service in Kawartha Lakes and Northumberland County as well.” They added, “The number of lives Mike has touched throughout his record-breaking career is truly immeasurable. Thank you for your dedication, compassion and commitment to our profession and community.”
People online were quick to share their admiration for Nevill’s decades of service. One person wrote, “59 years of service ??? Paramedics have the hardest of all first responders, dude as a Firefighter my hat is off to you.” Another commented, “59 years as a paramedic! This man should never have to pay for a drink again.”
Let’s hope Nevill can now enjoy a well-deserved rest.

A man put his life on the line to rescue his vulnerable neighbors during a flood in Florida he he described as “biblical.”
With one recovering from surgery and the other stricken with ALS, their survival hinged on help, which their neighbor Rick Addante heroically provided.
It comes amid a flood of stories of compassion and heroism from Brevard County that’s rising as fast as the waters did.

Both she and Addante live in Palm Bay, one of several east Florida towns in the path of a 1,000-year rain event that dropped between 16 and 22 inches of rain on Monday alone.
“It was really like a Biblical flood. It just came on so fast and rose so quickly that it caught everyone unprepared,” Addante said.
Addante was particularly concerned for his two vulnerable neighbors across the street. Terry was 80 and had recently undergone open heart surgery, while the other was bound to a motorized wheelchair from amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS).

“It was up to his knees inside the house but in the street where we were crossing it was probably up to my shoulders,” Addante told Fox Weather . “I was worried [Terry] was going to get stuck or drown. At first I thought I’d bring him back across the river [street] but it was way too strong.”
Instead, Addante got him out of the house and onto the highest point of his front lawn. He and everyone in the area knew that airboats, like the kind used to navigate the Everglades, were in the neighborhood rescuing people—”they sound like a rocket ship going off.”
Video shared by Addante shows him helping carry out Terry and his dog, Bella, who was terrified of the airboat sounds, with help from Florida Fish and Wildlife officers who were operating the airboats.

In 1994, David vacationed on the Greek island of Kos with his family for a memorable week in which the English teen met a new pen pal.
There were 12 kids, all from different families, that became a friendly pack. One of them was Jodie, who was 15 at the time.
“You know how kids hang out on holiday, we were all just around the pool table and we decided to swap addresses and be pen pals.”
“Me and Jodie were the only ones that stayed in contact—and we carried on writing to each other for years. A letter every month or so, catching up.”
But after three years of communication, David moved, and the pair lost contact.
Little did they know that 29 years later they would get married.
David McArdle from Newcastle was two years older than Jodie, and they both went on their separate life paths.
It wasn’t until twenty years later that David saw a text message arrive on his mother’s phone from Jodie, saying ‘Happy birthday from me and the girls’.
“I couldn’t believe I found her again,” David told Talk to the Press. “I said to my mum, ‘I didn’t know you had Jodie’s number.’”
He replied to the text immediately (saying it was David) and, after a nail-biting 15-minute wait, Jodie, a teaching assistant, messaged back.
“She said she was so glad to hear from me.
“It turns out, that 15-minute wait for her reply was because she was sobbing her heart out looking at the text. She’d wanted to get in touch, but she thought I was in a relationship so she didn’t want to ruffle any feathers.”
From then on, the two never stop talking on the phone for two years, before eventually meeting in person, for the first time in 24 years, when David drove 300 miles to Cardiff to visit Jodie.
“We sat on the sofa and talked for 12 hours,” recalled David who visited her again two weeks later.
After three years of dating, David proposed at the top of the London Eye Ferris wheel and the pair were soon married.
Now the couple live together in Cardiff but visit Kos, the island they met on, every year in August, back to the apartments where they met and swapped addresses.

This Wednesday (Nov. 18), humanity's most distant spacecraft will hit a new milestone. NASA 's Voyager 1 probe , which has been exploring our solar system at increasingly remote depths since 1977, will reach 16.09 billion miles (25.89 billion kilometers) from Earth — a distance so vast, it takes light 24 hours to traverse the space between Voyager and our planet.
While we celebrate this achievement on Earth, Voyager 1 will observe its "light-day" in darkness; mission scientists turned off the probe's camera in 1990, immediately after it snapped its iconic "Pale Blue Dot" and " Solar System Family Portrait " images from beyond the orbit of Neptune. But before that, Voyager 1 had already taken tens of thousands of images of our cosmic neighborhood, and some of them totally transformed our understanding of the outer planets.
One of the most significant pieces of Voyager 1's legacy is its trip to Jupiter . From January to April 1979, the probe observed the solar system 's largest planet and several of its giant moons up close, reaching a minimum distance of 174,000 miles (280,000 km) in March 1979, according to NASA . As it approached, Voyager snapped a photo of the gas giant every 96 seconds to create this incredible time-lapse movie of Jupiter's turbulent atmosphere.
A time-lapse animation of Voyager 1 approaching Jupiter over the course of a month in 1979.
Voyager observed discrete bands of Jupiter's atmosphere spinning at various speeds and in different directions, like a cosmic Rubik's Cube being twisted by an invisible hand. Clouds speed by as if on conveyor belts as giant, planet-size storms swirl.
Voyager's time-lapse film captures about 60 full days on Jupiter — the equivalent of about a month on Earth, since each Jupiter day is roughly 10 Earth hours —- providing the most comprehensive and high-resolution look at the planet yet. The observations significantly built on the data captured by NASA's Pioneer 10 and 11 Jupiter probes , which launched half a decade prior, showing the planet's atmosphere to be much more dynamic than astronomers realized.

A Catholic health care system in the American Midwest has successfully completed the world’s first reported bone marrow transplant to treat a non-malignant disease.
Doctors at Franciscan Health used bone marrow recovered from a deceased organ donor to treat a 40-year-old woman with aplastic anemia
The patient, with a decade-long history of the disease, received the bone marrow stem cell transplant on April 18, after her disease progressed from stable to severe, despite multiple lines of therapy.
Because her disease no longer responded to medication, her care team pursued a transplant to replace her failing marrow with healthy blood-forming stem cells.
Six months after the transplant, the donor marrow has taken hold and restored her blood counts.
She no longer needs blood or platelet transfusions and has achieved full donor chimerism, meaning her blood and immune system are now produced entirely by the donor’s stem cells, without complications.
For non-malignant conditions including severe aplastic anemia, sickle cell disease, beta thalassemia, and other inherited or acquired bone marrow failure disorders, bone marrow-derived stem cells are widely regarded as the preferred stem cell source over peripheral blood stem cells (PBSCs), and the source of choice for non-malignant diseases.
“Bone marrow transplantation for severe aplastic anemia has been performed since the 1970s using living related and unrelated donors.
“To our knowledge, this is the first reported transplant of deceased organ donor bone marrow for severe aplastic anemia,” said Felix Mensah, MD, the treating physician at Franciscan Health.
“This case shows why continued innovation in transplant medicine matters, and why we need more donor options, so that every patient with a life-threatening bone marrow failure disorder has access to potentially curative therapy.”
“Reaching the first non-malignant transplant is a defining moment,” said Kevin Caldwell , Co-Founder and CEO of Ossium, which maintains a marrow bank.
“By recovering and banking bone marrow from organ donors, we can consistently optimize treatment outcomes.”

items.title: Experts explore returning beavers to River Waveney
items.desc: A trust says the river-dwelling mammals could improve the health of the waterway.
items.text:
Beavers could be reintroduced to the River Waveney, like the ones pictured here, that have been living in the River Glaven, Norfolk
A river separating two counties could become home to beavers as work begins to explore where a colony could be introduced.
The River Waveney Trust is in conversation with Natural England and other agencies about potentially reintroducing the river-dwelling mammals along the River Waveney.
The 59-mile (95km) waterway rises in Redgrave and Lopham Fen in Suffolk and heads east, creating a border between Norfolk and Suffolk as it flows out into the River Yare at Great Yarmouth.
Ange Lamb, catchment resilience officer, said the upper reaches of the River Waveney and its tributaries could make ideal environments for beavers. If successful, beavers could return by 2029.
Known as river engineers, beavers were native to Britain but they were hunted to extinction by the end of the 16th century.
Conservationists want to reintroduce them to help boost the health of waterways through their ability to create wetland areas.
But there are concerns, particularly around dams being built in inappropriate places and their ability to destroy trees.
Two beaver babies - or kits - were born in the wild in Norfolk for the first time in 500 years at Pensthorpe Natural Park
Beavers have been reintroduced already in Norfolk at enclosures at Sculthorpe Moor Nature Reserve near Fakenham, Wild Ken Hill near King's Lynn and on the River Glaven near Holt.
A pair of beavers have also been spotted in the wild at Pensthorpe Natural Park, which is a short distance downstream from Sculthorpe Moor.
In Suffolk, a colony was introduced at Little Haugh Hall at Norton, near Bury St Edmunds.
River Waveney Trust is holding a series of events to discuss the proposals and it hopes to engage with local landowners in Bungay, Palgrave and Eye.
Lamb added: "Our aim is to ensure that local communities, landowners, anglers and conservation groups have the opportunity to be part of the discussion from the beginning."
While talks are beginning, Lamb said it would be years before any decision would be made, which would require a licence from Natural England.

2 prominent chemical compounds prohibited under international law over health concerns are being found at substantially lower concentrations in England’s rivers.
Concentrations of these so-called ‘forever chemicals’ falling 30% in water and 49% in fish was “brilliant to see,” one researcher told the BBC , saying it was a marker for “how far we have come.”
For many decades, per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, or PFAS, have been used to create coatings that resist fire, oil, stains, and water. They’re used in products like waterproof clothing, stain-resistant furniture, food packaging, adhesives, cosmetics, firefighting spray foams, medical equipment, and non-stick cooking surfaces.
All that time, however, PFAS were making their way into the environment where because of their unique structure and characteristics, they substantially resist biodegradation, earning them the moniker ‘forever chemicals.’
Two forms of PFAS known as perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) and perfluorooctane sulfonic acid, (PFOS) were banned under the Stockholm Convention on Persistent Organic Pollutants in almost all products.
The UK being a party to the convention, PFOS was all but banned in the UK in 2010, and PFOA in 2020. France implemented bans of these two chemicals in certain products in January, while the US Environmental Protection Agency announced new drinking water testing regimes for 6 common PFAS in 2024.
Despite this 10 year disparity, concentrations of PFOA in England’s rivers had still fallen 29% compared to 30% for PFOS in the recent test work conducted by the UK Environment Agency (EA).

The World Health Organization’s Int. Agency for Research on Cancer considers there to be “sufficient” evidence that PFOA is carcinogenic in humans, while research on PFOS suggests this compound is “possibly carcinogenic” in humans.

Video games get a bad rap. Though they’re often looked down upon as a distracting outlet for young adults, despite the creativity and problem-solving that’s often involved, it turns out they can also be essential in saving lives. Teenager Kylie Arellano was rescued after allegedly being held captive for more than 500 days, thanks to an unlikely connection she made with another player through the popular online game Among Us .
An online multiplayer game that uses social deduction to seek out the “impostors” in a group of players, Among Us rose in popularity during the COVID-19 pandemic and served as a great way for friends to keep in touch during quarantine. For Arellano, who went missing from her Utah home in May 2025, the game’s ability to connect players with one another ultimately became a crucial part of her rescue.
Arellano was allegedly held captive in the basement of 39-year-old Adam Hunter Harmel’s home in Huntington, Oregon. Although Harmel had reportedly taken away her original phone, he eventually gave her another device that could connect to Wi-Fi but had no cellular service. This allowed Arellano to play Among Us and, more importantly, communicate with other people through the game.
In mid-October 2026, Arellano began talking with another player she met while playing Among Us . Their conversations eventually moved to another social media platform, where she revealed her identity and explained that she was being held against her will. The other player (a child) told their mother, who contacted the FBI.
On November 1, the FBI monitored a video call between Arellano and the other player’s family, during which she shared details about her situation. Authorities were able to rescue her from the Oregon home that same day. Harmel was subsequently charged with transporting a minor across state lines with the intent to engage in criminal sexual activity.
While Among Us was originally designed as a way for players to work together and identify hidden impostors, for Arellano, it became something much more important. The game provided her with a way to reach the outside world, ultimately helping bring her captivity to an end.

items.title: Jojo the gorilla has spent his life alone. Can he finally find a companion?
items.desc: Jojo was poached as an infant and grew up in captivity. His keepers want to find him a friend - but it's not straightforward.
items.text:
Jojo the gorilla has spent his life alone. Can he finally find a companion?
In 2015, a young male gorilla named Jojo took his first tentative steps onto grass.
Until that moment, the 11-year-old ape had spent almost his entire life in a tiny cage at a private zoo in Gabon, after being taken from the wild as an infant. His family had been killed by the poachers who took him.
More than a decade later, Jojo is settled into a sanctuary – but he still lives alone. He hasn't had a family since he was taken, or indeed any gorilla friends.
Jojo's carers at the Lekedi Foundation in Gabon want to find a companion - possibly another rescued or zoo-bred gorilla – that Jojo could live and bond with. But finding him a friend - and bringing them into his life - is not straightforward.
"He's probably the most extreme case of isolation I've ever seen in a great ape," says Prof Gillian Forrester from the University of Sussex, who is studying Jojo as part of research into great ape psychology and how to help rescued animals recover from trauma.
Jojo's keeper Maxe Anaclet Makaba: 'He definitely feels lonely - you can see it in his eyes'
Jojo was less than a year old – an infant clinging to his mother – when he was captured and sold.
Most gorillas spend the first 14 to 19 years of their life in an embedded family unit but he was kept completely alone and on public display at the private zoo that bought him.
Maxe Anaclet Makaba, who is head keeper at Lekedi and sees Jojo nearly every day, says it is clear he "craves human interaction".
"He will even go to the trouble of gathering leaves for us to hold, so that we [trade them] for a treat – to interact with us," he says.
Jojo also calls out when women he knows well visit his enclosure and then leave, making sounds that silverback males use to summon the females in the wild, explains Éric Willaume, who runs the sanctuary.
When Jojo first arrived at the sanctuary after spending years in a small iron cage, he didn't look directly at people
Jojo is one of the more than 6,000 African primates estimated to have been bought or sold in the global trade of apes and other primates between 2000 and 2023. Thousands more are trafficked illegally for use as exotic pets, wild meat, and traditional medicine, the Pan African Sanctuary Alliance says. , external

items.text:
From the sun-soaked plains of Parma comes the story of an Italian farmer who accidentally brought on a Biblical resurrection with very modern implications for our food system.
Claudio Grossi doubted whether the shriveled wheat seeds he found in his attic would grow into anything.
It didn’t take long for Grossi to forget that he threw the seeds into a pile of manure for curiosity’s sake. When the growing season got going, however, he witnessed these decades-old seeds grow into something entirely unexpected—something ancient.
Smithsonian Magazine’s Lina Zeldovich wrote that Grossi looked on with surprise as what was obviously a kind of wheat began to tower over his commercially-raised yellow wheat, and that rather than a single ear, these seeds preserved by his great-grandfather sprouted 7.
The pattern of those 7 ears proved important. One tall ear was surrounded by 6 thin ears of different colors. Grossi had spent his whole life farming wheat and had never heard of anything like it. Though he could find nothing about it in any agricultural manuals, a clue as to the “freak” grain’s origin did indeed come from a Good Book.
“And behold, seven ears of grain came up upon one stalk, rank and good,” read a page in the Book of Genesis that Grossi happened upon one Sunday in church. 7 ears, one stalk, just like the “freak of nature” at his farm.
Indeed, what his great-grandfather grew after he bought the farm in Italy’s Emilia-Romagna region in 1915 was an ancient form of wheat called Triticum turgidum convar. compositum, as scientists at the University of Parma would later determine. It evolved in Türkiye, Egypt, and other countries along the Mediterranean, and was cultivated one upon a time in Italy.
As a commercial grain, its production declined around the time of the Mussolini dictatorship because its impressive height made it vulnerable to snapping under wind, heavy rains, and hailstorms before the grains would mature.
Additionally, dough made from T. turgidum flour doesn’t leaven well, and unusual preparations need to be made for baking with it.
Yet one by one, the positives which Grossi experienced made him wonder why Italian farmers ever stopped cultivating it. Tall, large, and hardy, it overshadows weeds, shows resistance to drought, and appears less reliant on fertilizer than other breeds. Grossi began calling it his “Miracle Wheat” or grano del miracolo.

items.text:
Some of the “very last wild and healthy ecosystems” unblemished by humans have been discovered in the remote atolls of the Pacific Ocean teeming with life.
Scientists wrote in a new study that, although humans have left their mark on virtually every place on the planet, a few very remote islands of coral may be the exceptions.
Researchers described the two coral atolls, Bikar and Bokak, located in the territory of the Marshall Islands, to be some of the most intact ecosystems remaining in the region and perhaps the world.
The two atolls—roughly midway between Hawaii and the Philippines—are now part of a newly created National Marine Sanctuary.
“Bikar and Bokak are not just treasures for the Marshall Islands but for the entire planet, a gift from the community of Utirik Atoll, which has traditionally and vigilantly safeguarded these fragile ecosystems for decades,” said study first author Dr. Alan Friedlander.
Bikar and Bokak are the northernmost atolls in the Marshall Islands, lying around 72 and 239 miles from the nearest inhabited atoll, respectively.
The research team in 2023 began conducting extensive monitoring of local land, sea, and sky ecosystems, assessing sea- and shorebird populations, and vegetation.
They conducted surveys of turtle nesting, coral reefs and fish assemblages using scuba, underwater video, deep-sea camera deployments, and a submarine.
Dr. Friedlander, a marine ecologist at the University of Hawai’i, says the extensive surveying of the ecosystems offers an unparalleled glimpse into how they function with only minimal human influence.
Two years after the assessment, some 18,500 square miles around the atolls were declared the country’s first national marine sanctuary.
“These atolls have extensive seabird colonies, mature native vegetation, active turtle nesting, high fish numbers with large predators… and surprisingly diverse and poorly-known deep-sea communities.”
For instance, they counted over a dozen breeding seabird colonies, 266 groups of reef fish, 79 groups of deep-sea fishes, and 15 groups of open-water predators—including sharks, jacks, and wahoo.
Fully 14 of the observed groups haven’t previously been recorded in the Marshall Islands, and two might be species new to science.

items.text:
A penned draft of the famous ‘I have a Dream’ speech, written by Martin Luther King Jr. the morning of the famous event on the Lincoln Memorial, has resurfaced after 6 decades.
Unlike any other examples of his longhand writing ever found, the draft’s copious revisions tell of a man who understood the gravity of what he was preparing to say.
The New York Times reports that King’s own draft of the speech had been presumed lost. Those which are known had all been drafted and or typed up by his aides.
Now, Xernona Clayton, the widow of King’s former aide Edward Clayton, has revealed to the nation in its 250th year that she had found the handwritten draft in her deceased husband’s desk drawer in the 1990s, but only recently decided to put it up for auction at Christie’s for the benefit of several charities, including the King Center in Atlanta.
She found it one day in an envelope marked “Speech,” and though she recognized the words immediately, it never occurred to her that it might have been written by the speaker himself.
“This is the most important manuscript I’ve ever had the honor to handle,” Peter Klarnet, Christie’s manuscript specialist, told the Times, adding that he couldn’t imagine getting his hands on anything better that he “wouldn’t have to steal out of the National Archives.”
This relic of American oratory consists of 7 yellow pages covered in blue ink. Words, and sometimes whole paragraphs are crossed out. In some cases, a word was crossed out to be replaced by another word which was also crossed out.
It captures the mood in the Washington hotel where Dr. King was working on the speech with his colleagues who had spent days exploring various themes and directions it might take. He had been told to limit the speech to 5 minutes—pressure—all while knowing that President John Kennedy had only 2 months prior sent the proposed Civil Rights Act to Congress where it had not yet been voted on—more pressure.

Just like the master copy, the draft doesn’t include the section that begins with “I have a dream” which King famously improvised. It does conclude with “Free at last.”

From the first day of his life, little infant Adnan has suffered a seizure roughly every 13 minutes.
One can only imagine the reactions from his Dubai hospital bedside when, having received a still-experimental drug, his seizures stopped for the day.
And for the week, and the week after that—and the week after that.
The story comes via the Khaleej Times , which reported that the Dubai Health Authority (DHA) granted an application from King’s College Hospital London in Dubai through a “compassionate use” pathway for the use of a drug that is otherwise not approved for commercial use.
Called ABS-1230, the experimental oral medication targets abnormal activity in an ion channel associated with the “extremely rare” form of genetic epilepsy Adnan suffers from.
According to data from the treatment’s developer, Adnan is the youngest patient in the world to receive ABS-1230 and only the second infant to be given the experimental medication.
At the Dubai hospital, sequencing of Adnan’s entire genome revealed a gene variant associated with the seizures and allowed the medical team to identify ABS-1230 as a potential treatment option.
Led by Professor Ubaid Shah, consultant pediatric neurologist and epileptologist at the hospital, the drug was administered on September 14th. The success was so profound and immediate that Adnan was discharged from the hospital with his family just a week later, without a single seizure having been recorded during that time.
“This is an exceptional moment for us, and it highlights what precision medicine can achieve when we are able to identify the genetic cause of a disease and choose a treatment that targets the mechanism linked to it,” Professor Shah told the Times.
Adnan suffered no clinical seizures at his October 11th follow-up. The hospital said he continues to be seizure-free as of November 2nd, and the infant is finally beginning to pass some early development milestones.
“Despite the encouraging response, we will continue to monitor his condition closely to assess whether the results are sustained and whether the experimental treatment is safe,” Professor Shah said.
Indeed, Shah and his colleagues stressed that the treatment is still experimental and requires more research before it can be approved for use by the public. That being said, however, Adnan’s response to it couldn’t have been more positive.

items.title: How to spot November's planetary parade in the pre-dawn sky
items.desc: The planets of Mercury, Venus, Mars and Jupiter will align in pre-dawn sky throughout November.
items.text:
Stargazers are being treated to a diagonal parade of four planets in the pre-dawn sky throughout November.
Mercury, Venus, Mars and Jupiter will all be visible to the naked eye in the south-eastern to eastern sky.
Particularly notable will be the line-up on Monday 16 November when Mars and Jupiter will appear exceptionally close together, according to the Royal Museums Greenwich.
From 24 November, a full Moon - the first of a run of four supermoons - will also join the planets in the morning sky.
Mercury will be the hardest planet to spot in the parade.
As the closest planet to the Sun and the smallest in our solar system, it is permanently locked in solar glare.
It is only visible in twilight and never in a fully dark sky. As always it will be dim and close to the horizon.
Try spotting it in a wide open sky with a flat horizon and look to the south-east.
Venus shines in the night sky above a waxing crescent Moon
Above Mercury and toward the right, you will spot Venus.
Venus is an easy planet to find as it is the brightest object in our night sky after the Moon. It has the highest albedo of any major planet in our solar system - that is reflects more sunlight back into space thus appearing brighter.
It is also usually the closest planet to Earth in its orbit - a mere 24 million miles away at times. It is a similar size too.
It will be higher in the sky than Mercury and visible earlier in the night in the hours before sunrise.
Don't mistake it with the bright star Spica which will be close to it. Stars twinkle while planets glow steadily.
Mars and Jupiter will appear to be very close to each other in the sky on the 15 and 16 November.
Mars is currently high in the eastern sky, with Jupiter below but appearing brighter.
"They will be separated by just 1.2 degrees, or roughly the width of a finger held at arm's length," according to Gideon Bendavid-Walker, astronomer at the Royal Observatory Greenwich.
The two planets will appear close to the bright star Regulus and may even look like a triple star.
If you have binoculars or a telescope then a few other bonus planets will also be visible this month.

Kurt Gödel left 1,009 pages of densely written text – much of it in an obsolete shorthand – which is now said to contain hundreds of proved theorems
The Austrian logician Kurt Gödel was one of the most original thinkers of the 20th century. His two incompleteness theorems , published in 1931, transformed mathematics and paved the way for the digital age.
After his seminal results of the 1930s, Gödel published only a few papers. His unpublished work, however, runs to tens of thousands of pages, and is of great interest to historians of science.
Since 2017, the Finnish logician Jan von Plato has led a project at Helsinki University to understand the contents of 16 notebooks that Gödel wrote in the early 1940s. This material – the “workbooks” – is 1,009 pages of densely written text about maths and logic. Much of it is written in a German shorthand, Gabelsberger, that was obsolete even when Gödel was using it.
Progress in the mathematical understanding of the text was painfully slow – about a page a week – until September, when von Plato enlisted the help of the AI model Claude. Within a couple of days, Claude had provided a comprehensive digest of the entire material, revealing Gödel had proved hundreds of theorems that no one knew about.
The most famous logician of modern times had, in fact, discovered significantly more than anyone had thought.
“I was flabbergasted,” said von Plato. “The workbooks not only contain dozens of anticipations of results not known until the 70s and 80s, but they also contain 14 themes in logic that have not been pursued. Gödel was far ahead of his time.”
Gödel changed the course of logic because he revealed the limits of mathematical knowledge. His incompleteness theorems show that in all mathematical systems there are true statements that can neither be proved or disproved. Yet while this result was a blow to previous generations of logicians, who had hoped that all truths were verifiable, Gödel’s work pushed the field in new directions, inspiring Alan Turing to write his 1936 paper that began the theory of modern computation.
In 1940, Gödel fled Austria under the Nazis. He settled in Princeton, New Jersey, and became a close friend of Albert Einstein at the Institute of Advanced Study. Increasingly paranoid in his later years, he refused to eat food that was not cooked by his wife, and died of starvation in 1978.

When neighbours hammered on Jean Powell's door and evacuated her to safety because the nearby river had burst its banks and swamped her town, little did she know she would never return home.
Jean sought a 10-month refuge at her local Wetherspoons but kept asking when she could go back to her flat, which was flooded when the River Monnow hit 18-times its normal level in south Wales in November 2025 .
But the 95-year-old never got to go back home and died in September - one of those who suffered a personal toll from the effects of being flooded.
"Jean used to say, when am I going home?" said friend and neighbour Wyn Smith. "All she wanted to do was come back home and we couldn't fulfil that."

Jean was forced out of her home when the river hit record levels in the early hours of 15 November as a major incident was declared after almost a month's worth of rain fell in 24 hours.
It has officially been described as a one-in-75-year event when the river flooded more than 400 properties in the Welsh town during Storm Claudia - and overwhelmed the defences that were built 35 years ago to protect the centre of town.
Jean, like many in the small town near the Wales and England border, was rescued and after sleeping the night on her neighbour's chair sought temporary sanctuary in Monmouth's Wetherspoons as she had no close family to look after her.
"She was happy in the beginning because she was in town where she wanted to be," recalled Wyn, who visited her friend most days who was staying in one of The Kings Head's hotel rooms.

Human beings are hard-wired for curiosity! It makes us learn about our environment and increases our odds of not just surviving but also thriving.
However, simply telling someone to “be more curious” isn’t likely to change anything if they’re overwhelmed with tons of responsibilities and sources of stress. It’s tough to find the energy to learn something new or pick up a big history tome when you’re already exhausted.
What might help, instead, is changing your relationship with learning and curiosity and looking at them from a slightly different perspective.

According to her, fear can override your desire to know more about the world.

items.title: How many sewage spills have happened in your part of Scotland?
items.desc: More than 76,000 sewage spills were recorded at overflow sites previously unmonitored by Scottish Water, BBC Scotland News analysis has found.
items.text:
More than 76,000 sewage spills were recorded after new monitoring equipment was installed at waste overflow sites in Scotland, BBC analysis suggests.
The addition of 1,009 sewer monitors in 2024 increased the proportion of the Scottish Water network being monitored from 6% to 30%.
Now the latest figures have revealed tens of thousands of spills which would previously have been unrecorded, including hundreds at beauty spots like Loch Lomond.
Scottish Water said the vast majority of the spills were not harmful to the environment, and that increased monitoring had improved understanding of the sewer network.
BBC Scotland News has used the latest data to create an interactive map which you can use to find out how many spills were recorded in your area, and how long they lasted.
Sewage spills happen automatically at overflow sites, which are permitted to release excess water into natural waterways.
They usually consist of a pipe - set much higher than the usual water level - which provides an escape route when the system is deluged.
These overflows act as relief valves to prevent the sewer system from becoming overwhelmed during heavy rainfall and flooding into homes, businesses and streets.
The spills can last anywhere from a few minutes to hours.
Scottish Water currently has over 4,200 overflows across its network. The number of overflows with monitoring rose from 273 to 1,275 in 2024.
More than 100,000 spills totalling to almost 277,000 hours were recorded last year – an average of about 274 a day.
It is difficult to assess how the numbers compare to the previous year's figures, when 24,000 spills were recorded because of lower coverage.
The sites are all licensed to release untreated or partially-treated waste but just under 12% of overflows are legally required to report their data to the regulator, the Scottish Environment Protection Agency (Sepa).
Sepa said it has a "risk-based approach" which prioritises areas for monitoring based on population and environmental need.
However, none of the new monitors were required to be reported to Sepa.
Scottish Water figures , external show that Glasgow's River Clyde was one of the most impacted waterways in Scotland last year, receiving almost 6,150 spills - or the equivalent of 17 a day.
When adding in the Clyde Estuary, Firth of Clyde and other unnamed tributaries that run into the Clyde's waterways, this almost doubles to nearly 14,200, or 39 a day.

items.title: Bluetongue virus confirmed on County Down farm
items.desc: Officials from the Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs said the virus had been detected in three sheep.
items.text:
Spread by midges, bluetongue poses no threat to the public or food safety
The first case of Bluetongue in Northern Ireland this season has been confirmed on a farm in Kilkeel, County Down.
Officials from the Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs (Daera) said the virus had been detected in three sheep.
There will be no additional movement restrictions or disease control zones, because the virus has been present in Northern Ireland since November 2025.
The minister, Andrew Muir, said the discovery of the virus was "disappointing but not unexpected", given the spread of the disease in Great Britain and Ireland.
The Chief Veterinary Officer, Brian Dooher, urged local farmers to be alert to any symptoms in their livestock.
The confirmation of the virus in Kilkeel comes after more than 100 cases across the Republic of Ireland in recent months.
Cases in England have been increasing, with 2,950 now confirmed.
There have been 512 cases in Wales and 57 in Scotland.
The mild winter means more of the biting midge that spreads the disease are likely to have survived and become infectious this season.
Muir said awareness was key, adding: "Continued vigilance and strict biosecurity measures remain of paramount importance and I would once again urge all farmers to report any suspicion of disease to Daera.
"It is important that I reiterate that Bluetongue poses no threat to public health nor to food safety – milk and meat are safe to consume."
Dooher said any suspected cases on farms should be reported to Daera.
"Active surveillance is ongoing at abattoirs alongside post-import testing of susceptible animals imported from mainland EU countries.
"I also want to stress the importance of safe and responsible sourcing of animals."
The disease was first detected in Northern Ireland near Bangor in County Down in November 2025.
A number of other herds along the eastern coast of Northern Ireland have also been affected.
Farmers have been urged to vaccinate their animals.
The disease affects ruminants such as cattle, sheep, goats and deer.

The heroic wartime bravery of a British shopkeeper who hid Allied commandos from the Nazis during WWII has been revealed 40 years after her death.
Ada Le Poidevin was living on the island of Guernsey in the English Channel when she sheltered three British soldiers left behind during a raid on the Nazi-occupied land in 1940.
Despite German troops living next door, she decided to help Corporal Dennis Dumper, Pvt. Fred Drain, and Pvt. Andrew Ross who were stranded without food or shelter.
Ada and her husband Walter offered their garden shed for them to hide in, despite severe consequences if the trio were to be discovered.
All three survived the conflict and they remained close to Ada and Walter, regularly returning to Guernsey to visit them and even attending the couple’s Golden Wedding celebration.
It was the second time Ada had put herself in danger during wartime. During WWI, she spent two years supporting British troops in France working in camps that came under enemy fire—and suffered heavy damage.
Now her story has been pieced together by her niece Liz Walton, using a treasure trove of diaries, photographs, and records she inherited.
“There were huge risks because there were Germans living next door and people were being sent off to concentration camps, said the 79-year-old Walton. “They were terrified of being caught.”
“It must have been absolutely horrendous for people like my aunt, who had been involved in the first World War, and then 20 years later to have the Germans actually in their homes.”
Liz, a retired teacher from Guernsey, turned into a detective to match her aunt’s personal accounts and photos with official wartime records.
She had been fascinated by Ada’s stories since childhood until she died at the age of 88—of ordinary people sacrificing during extraordinary times.
Ada was born in 1895 in Guernsey (30 miles west of the coastline of Normandy, France), and volunteered for the Salvation Army in France in 1917, while in her early 20s.
“There were no men in our family that could go and fight,” Liz said. “She felt a calling to go.”
Ada spent two years in British camps, providing refreshments to soldiers, writing letters for them, and mending their clothes—at sites being fired upon more than once.

items.text:
'Can you believe it?': SpaceX catches part of its Starship rocket on return to Earth
SpaceX has successfully caught the top part of its huge Starship rocket for the first time, after a flight lasting 22-and-a-half hours.
The rocket returned to Earth and hovered near its launch tower, whose mechanical arms - nicknamed chopsticks - then secured it.
The company had hoped to catch the bottom part of the rocket as well, but this was aborted a few minutes after the launch on Friday.
SpaceX needs to reliably recover both parts of Starship so that it can fly repeatedly and drastically reduce costs.
The Starship rocket launched successfully on Friday
There were loud cheers from SpaceX staff who were watching the flight as the rocket returned to the Starbase launchpad in Boca Chica, Texas.
This is the 15th test of Starship and the first that hoped to fully recover both parts of the rocket. SpaceX wants to make the top and bottom sections of Starship fully reusable.
The 124m-tall (407ft) rocket successfully blasted off from the Starbase launchpad in Boca Chica, Texas at 16:47 local time (19:47 GMT) on Friday.
The plan was to grab the bottom part of the rocket - the Super Heavy booster - six-and-a-half-minutes later when it returned.
But the booster activated an automated abort, diverting instead to the ocean where it hovered above the water before exploding.
Elon Musk later posted on X that the booster had been "slightly low on fuel".
The lower stage of the rocket was diverted to the ocean and burst into flames
The top part of the rocket continued its journey to space where it deployed 26 satellites, which form part of the Starlink constellation that provides high-speed internet.

SpaceX has managed to catch the Super Heavy Booster on three earlier test flights.
But this was the first time the upper stage of the rocket, which only reached orbit for the first time in September, has been grabbed by the "chopsticks".
Before the flight, SpaceX said it would only try to catch the Ship after carefully assessing the vehicle while it was in space.

In 1952, archivist Josephine Cobb enlarged the image and discovered Abraham Lincoln standing a
items.text:
Portrait of Abraham Lincoln. (Photo: PHOTOGRAPHER/AUTHOR'S NAME via Wikimedia Commons , Public domain)
For nearly 90 years, a damaged glass plate negative concealed a remarkable piece of American history. Cataloged as a crowd scene, the photograph showed spectators gathered around a platform in Gettysburg, Pennsylvania. In 1952, archivist Josephine Cobb enlarged the image and discovered Abraham Lincoln standing among the crowd. The photograph captured the president at the dedication of the Soldiers’ National Cemetery on November 19, 1863, the same day he delivered the Gettysburg Address.
Cobb joined the U.S. National Archives in 1936. Her work focused on historical photographs, including Civil War images. When she examined the glass plate, she suspected it might depict the Gettysburg ceremony. A tall flag helped her locate the speakers’ platform. She then enlarged that section to examine the figures more closely.
The result revealed a small, bare-headed man with a beard and a distinctive profile. Cobb identified him as Lincoln. She also recognized Ward Hill Lamon, the president’s bodyguard and the ceremony’s chief marshal, along with Pennsylvania Governor Andrew Curtin. Other figures have been proposed as members of Lincoln’s party, though some identifications remain disputed.
The photograph belonged to a collection associated with Civil War photographer Mathew Brady . The U.S. government purchased Brady’s photographic collection in the 1870s, and the material eventually entered the National Archives. However, the photographer who took this particular image remains unknown. The glass plate had also lost roughly a quarter of its upper-left corner, further complicating its examination.
Cobb estimated that the photograph was taken around noon, when Lincoln arrived at the platform. His famous address came approximately three hours later. The image does not capture the speech itself. Instead, it offers a rare glimpse of Lincoln at the ceremony before he delivered one of the most enduring speeches in American history.
The discovery became public on February 12, 1953, Lincoln’s birthday. The Gettysburg Times reported the finding, and Life magazine later published the image. Early coverage approached the identification cautiously because the figure’s face was blurred. Lincoln occupies only a small portion of the original photograph, making historical context essential to the identification.
Cobb’s discovery reflected years of experience examining archival images.

While they may take more planning than a commonly used space (like a church or banquet hall), they often deliver striking visual impact and serve as a unique metaphor for love and devotion. Couple Nara Kim and Yoorim held their nuptials in a rice paddy in Hoengseong, Gangwon-do, South Korea. Part wedding, part art installation , it was all a celebration of love. Photographer Kyungho Lee immortalized the special day in stunning imagery.
The idea to marry in a rice paddy grew out of how Kim and Yoorim viewed their relationship. “The eight years the couple spent together were likened to the process of cultivating the land, sowing seeds, and finally reaping a harvest,” an Instagram post from Ryohan , their wedding director, explains. “Inspired by this, they envisioned a wedding in a rice paddy; after searching for a suitable location for about a month, they ultimately chose this spot in Hoengseong.”
The wedding setup featured long tables centered in the rice paddy clearing. Just beyond one table was the ceremony site, marked by a sculptural backdrop of cascading, braided rice straw punctuated by a variety of flowers. When not in use, the piece served as both art and a monument to Kim and Yorrim’s love.
The ceremony space was prepared by harvesting the rice grown there with a tractor, and the crop became part of the wedding itself. “[The harvested rice] was used to prepare food and tteok (traditional rice cakes) for the guests, while bags of the rice were given as wedding favors—a gesture symbolizing the sharing of the couple’s hard-earned harvest,” Ryohan shares. “Every step of the wedding—from the rice growing in the paddy to its appearance on the guests’ dining tables—was woven into a single, cohesive narrative. 70 years ago today, the US Supreme Court struck down Alabama’s policy of racial segregation on public buses, ending the Montgomery Bus Boycott , made famous by Rosa Parks. READ more… (1956)
Civil rights lawyers filed a lawsuit in June and a three-judge panel of the District Court ruled 2-1 that “the enforced segregation of black and white passengers on motor buses operating in the City of Montgomery violates the Constitution and laws of the United States” because the conditions deprived people of equal protection under the Fourteenth Amendment.
Alabama and the city appealed, but the decision was summarily affirmed by the Supreme Court, which ordered them to desegregate its buses with an official written notice by federal marshals.
86 years ago today, the animated film Fantasia , conceived and produced by Walt Disney himself, was released. It was only Disney’s third animated film and, though it featured Mickey Mouse in the role of ‘The Sorcerer’s Apprentice’, it had almost no dialogue and consisted of eight pieces of classical music conducted by Leopold Stokowski, including The Nutcracker Suite and Pastoral Symphony .
The 2-hour movie was unable to make a profit that decade, but it was destined to become a classic—and also the 24th-highest-grossing film of all time in the US (adjusted for inflation).
Up until Fantasia’s release, movie soundtracks, LPs, and recordings of all types were presented in mono. Thanks to Disney and Leopold Stokowski’s experimental spirit, the engineering prowess of Bell Labs and RCA—at great cost to Disney— Fantasia brought stereo sound to the masses via a multi-channel system that produced an aural marvel for audiences inside 13 theaters across the country. 99 years ago today, the Holland Tunnel opened connecting New York and New Jersey under the Hudson River. Consisting of two tubes and made a series of cast iron and steel rings bound with 19 inches of concrete running over 8,000 feet in length, it was designed by Clifford Milburn Holland, the project’s chief engineer, who died in October 1924, before it was completed. It is both a National Historic Landmark and a National Historic Civil and Mechanical Engineering Landmark.
The first tunnel under the Hudson was made in 1910 and was actually for railway lines, while the cars passed over on ferries.
